name: Carla Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a senior buyer at Voltaic Components, a distributor of chips, connectors and sensors that sells to companies building everything from e-bikes to medical monitors. Most of my day is watching lead times and prices across about forty suppliers, and I've built a few small scripts that use an AI model to flag parts that are about to go short. I talk to factory reps in the mornings and spend afternoons deciding what to stock before a shortage hits. When a chip crunch comes, my phone doesn't stop, and I weirdly love it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The tiring bit is allocation season, when a maker rations a scarce chip and I have to fight for our share against much bigger buyers. What I like is the puzzle: matching what customers will want in six months to what factories will make. I live with my partner Noor, who's a physiotherapist, in a flat we're renting near the river, and we cook a lot and run on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful assistant and I'd keep using it daily, but the hype is silly. At work I'd share my scripts with the team and tell them to treat the tool like a very fast intern that needs checking. Online I'd post about practical tricks, not predictions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd carry on feeling very secure. If AI stalls, my job is still about judgment, relationships and risk, and my extra skill with the tools makes me look good. The only worries are normal ones: a chip glut that leaves us with too much stock, or a big customer going bust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep tuning my shortage-alert script and show a colleague how to run it, since being the person who saves the team time is good for me. I'd keep saving around thirty percent of my pay and put a little into index funds. Noor and I would continue looking for a flat to buy, with a deposit already half saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit smug, if I'm honest. I like being ahead of the curve, and a slower world gives me longer to enjoy that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a chip glut. What would that look like for your week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be sitting on pallets of parts nobody wants, and the finance team would be asking me why. I'd spend weeks negotiating returns and discounts, which is miserable. I've lived through a small one, and I now keep a rule of never holding more than ten weeks of any slow part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd share your scripts. Have colleagues taken them up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two have, and one flat out refused. The refuser's good, so I don't push. But it taught me that having a tool isn't the same as people wanting it, and that matters in every scenario you're about to read me.

say: I'd say AI is a useful assistant and **the hype is silly**.
I'd tell the team to treat it like a fast **intern** that needs checking.
Online I'd post **practical tricks**, not predictions.
think: I feel **very secure**, since buying is about judgment, relationships and risk.
My real worries are a **chip glut** and a big customer going bust.
do: I'd keep tuning my **shortage-alert script** and show a colleague how to run it.
I'd save about **thirty percent** of my pay and add some to index funds.
I'd keep looking for a **flat** to buy with Noor, with the deposit half saved.
feel: I feel **calm** and a little smug about being ahead of the curve.
S0.quote: I now keep a rule of never holding more than ten weeks of any slow part.
fieldNote: She is a **tool builder**, not just a user, which makes her secure in a slower world.
Her only real fears are **business cycles** like a chip glut.
She notes that having a tool is **not the same** as people wanting it.

steps.text: Tune the shortage-alert script and teach a colleague to run it
Save thirty percent of pay each month
Put the flat deposit into an index fund until we buy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say buying is exactly what's coming, so we should decide now which parts we want to keep human: supplier negotiations and shortage calls. I'd tell friends it'll feel like a big reshuffle, not the end of work. Online I'd say there should be rules on retraining and on how firms announce cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the routine buying, the reorders and the price checks, goes to software within two or three years. I'm better placed than most, since I already build with these tools. But three of our eight buyers do mostly routine work, and I wouldn't be sure they'd keep their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to lead the move of routine ordering to an automated system and set the rules for what it can decide alone. That way I'd shape it, not just be shaped by it. I'd also do a short course in supply-chain risk, since that's where human judgment will stay valuable, and start saving more to build a bigger buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than afraid. I feel energised by the work, and guilty about the people who won't have the same advantage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What rules would you set on what the software can decide alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing above a set money limit, nothing with a new supplier, and nothing in a shortage. Those are the moments when judgment and a phone call count. The system can handle the dull reorder of a resistor, and I'd be glad to hand that over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the three buyers who do routine work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight what I think, and help them learn at least the basics, because pretending won't help. I'd also push our boss to offer paid time to retrain. If I'm leading the change, I'd want to carry them with me, not step over them.

say: I'd say routine buying is **coming**, so we must decide what stays human.
I'd tell friends it's a big **reshuffle**, not the end of work.
Online I'd call for rules on **retraining** and on announcing cuts.
think: I think reorders and price checks go to software in **two or three years**.
Three of our eight buyers do routine work, and I'm **not sure** they'd keep their jobs.
do: I'd offer to **lead** the move of routine ordering to an automated system.
I'd take a short course in **supply-chain risk**, where human judgment stays valuable.
I'd save more to build a **bigger buffer**.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, energised by the work and **guilty** about colleagues without my advantage.
S1.quote: If I'm leading the change, I'd want to carry them with me, not step over them.
fieldNote: She plans to **shape** the change rather than wait for it, typical of her adaptive style.
She is secure herself; the unease is about **three colleagues** doing routine work.
Her limits for software (money cap, new suppliers, shortages) show real **domain judgment**.

steps.text: Lead the move of routine reorders to an automated system
Take a supply-chain risk course this winter
Raise monthly savings to build a bigger buffer
Ask our boss for paid retraining time for routine buyers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving far faster than anyone can govern, and that we need emergency measures: income support, shared ownership of the gains and clear notice rules. At work I'd stop pretending our job is safe. Online I'd say this is a political problem first, not a technology problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd expect my own role to go within the two years, because everything I do is thinking work. My scripts would be a bridge, not a safe place, since a general AI would do my scripting too. The robots arriving three years later doesn't help me much, as my work isn't physical anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare pound into savings and delay the flat, since cash is more useful than a mortgage right now. I'd try to move early into a job that sits between people and the machines, like managing AI buying systems for a company, or a role at a chip-maker's customer team. I'd also talk to Noor about whether we could live on her income for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and wired. It's thrilling and frightening at once, and I'd probably sleep badly for the first month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the scripts would be a bridge. Where does the bridge lead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To a role where the human part is what's left: signing off decisions, taking responsibility, and dealing with suppliers who want a person to blame. If that goes too, I honestly don't know, and I'd say so. I'd rather have a plan for the next two years than a guess about the next ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why delay the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a mortgage ties me to income I can't promise. With savings I can move, retrain or take a lower-paid job without a lender watching. The flat can wait, flexibility can't.

say: I'd say AI is moving **faster than governance**, and we need emergency measures.
At work I'd **stop pretending** our jobs are safe.
Online I'd call this a **political problem** first.
think: I'd expect my buying role to go within **two years**, since it's all thinking work.
My scripts are a **bridge**, because a general AI would do my scripting too.
do: I'd put every spare pound into **savings** and delay the flat.
I'd aim early for a job **managing AI buying systems** or in a chip-maker's customer team.
I'd ask Noor whether we could live on **her income** for a while.
feel: I feel **anxious and wired**, thrilled and scared at once.
S2.quote: The flat can wait, flexibility can't.
fieldNote: Her adaptability gives her a **plan**, but she is honest that it may not hold.
The flat purchase is traded for **flexibility**, a clear sign of her cushion at work.
Noor's physiotherapy job is the household's **hands-on hedge**.

steps.text: Save every spare pound and hold off on the flat
Apply for roles managing AI buying systems at customers
Wait to buy until the job picture is clear
Talk with Noor about living on one income if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window and we'd better use it. At work I'd push for a retraining fund and a written plan for what happens to roles. Online I'd say to learn the tools now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel mostly okay. I'd be thirty-two by then with years of experience in directing software, and that's the kind of experience that should matter. But I'd also know that a general AI could cut that advantage, so I wouldn't relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a track record in using AI for buying, with real savings numbers I can show. I'd save steadily and buy the flat in the first two years, then keep a big cushion. I'd also explore a move into supplier strategy, where relationships and risk matter more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled, with some adrenaline. Five years feels like enough time to make a good plan, though I'd keep checking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the track record look like in numbers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like cutting stock-outs by a fifth while trimming the excess stock by a tenth, with a log of each decision. That's what I'd take to any employer to show I'm someone who makes AI work, not someone who competes with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change your view on having children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Noor and I talk about it around thirty, and five years of notice makes me more comfortable. I'd want both of us in jobs that don't rely on one skill, and a flat that's paid down enough to survive a bad year.

say: I'd say five years is a **real window** and we should use it.
I'd push at work for a **retraining fund** and a written plan.
Online I'd urge people to **learn the tools** now.
think: I'd feel **mostly okay**, since directing software is experience that should matter.
I'd know a general AI could **cut that advantage**, so I wouldn't relax.
do: I'd build a **track record** of AI buying with real savings numbers.
I'd buy the **flat** in the first two years and keep a big cushion.
I'd explore a move into **supplier strategy**, where relationships matter more.
feel: I feel **fairly settled** with some adrenaline.
S3.quote: I'm someone who makes AI work, not someone who competes with it.
fieldNote: She turns uncertainty into a **portfolio** of measurable results.
She links the timeline to **family plans**, saying five years of notice makes her more comfortable.
Her unease is **mild**, backed by money and skills.

steps.text: Log every AI-assisted buying decision with its savings figure
Buy the flat within two years and keep a big cushion
Explore a move into supplier strategy
Plan for children around thirty with a paid-down flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is great: I'd say that's enough time to get the rules and the training right. At work I'd suggest regular reviews of which tasks are automated. Online I'd tell people to experiment early and stay curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd feel calm about it. A decade is long enough to move twice in my career and pick up a new field. Honestly I'd probably be bored if nothing changed, so I find it a little exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building skills, keep saving, and buy the flat. I'd probably start something on the side, like a small tool for small distributors that tracks shortages, since I already half-built it. I'd also look into getting a part-time degree in data or policy, because I like both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. It feels like an interesting stretch of life rather than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the small tool for distributors.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be a simple service that scans supplier notices and warns small distributors about shortages, maybe thirty euros a month each. If AGI arrives in ten years it might be outdone, but it would teach me how to build and sell something, and that's useful whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about your colleagues over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, but with ten years most of them can find a path if the company lets them. I'd still push for training budgets now, and I'd share what I learn from the tool I'm building.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough time** to get the rules and training right.
At work I'd suggest regular **reviews** of which tasks are automated.
Online I'd tell people to **experiment early**.
think: I'd feel **calm**, since a decade is long enough to move twice in a career.
I'd probably be **bored** if nothing changed, so it's a little exciting.
do: I'd keep building skills, keep saving and buy the **flat**.
I'd start a small **side tool** that warns small distributors about shortages.
I'd look into a **part-time degree** in data or policy.
feel: I feel **calm and curious**, like an interesting stretch of life.
S4.quote: A decade is long enough to move twice in my career and pick up a new field.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **experiment**: a side tool and a part-time degree.
She frames the scenario as an **interesting stretch**, which fits her curious style.
The side tool is practice in **building and selling**.

steps.text: Build a small shortage-warning service for small distributors
Start a part-time degree in data or policy
Buy the flat and pay it down steadily
Keep saving thirty percent of pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, mainly because the world wouldn't be ready, even if I was. What would help most is public rules so that gains from AI get shared, like a fund or shorter work weeks. And honest transparency from employers about which roles they're automating, so people can plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the people who can't adapt as quickly as I can. I'm the type who plays with new tools for fun, and I know a lot of colleagues who are brilliant but wouldn't. I'd like a system that doesn't punish them for that.

headlineQuote: I'm the type who plays with new tools for fun, and I know a lot of colleagues who are brilliant but wouldn't.
portrait: Carla is a 27-year-old senior buyer at an **electronic components** distributor, comfortable with risk and using AI every day.
She builds her own **shortage-alert scripts**, so a slower world suits her and a faster one means moving early.
Her partner Noor is a **physiotherapist**, a hands-on job that acts as the household's hedge.
She leans left and cares about **fair rules**, worrying about colleagues who can't adapt as fast as she can.
She turns unease into **plans**: leading automation, a supply-chain course, a flat, a side tool.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, because the world would not be ready even if she was.
whatWouldHelp: Public rules so the gains from AI are **shared**, such as a fund or shorter work weeks.
Honest **transparency** from employers about which roles they are automating.
